claims.text: Atomic size mismatch and mixing enthalpy govern the reliable formation of noble metal–based HEA nanomaterials.
Atomic size mismatch and mixing enthalpy govern the catalytic performance of noble metal–based HEA nanomaterials.
Atomic size mismatch and mixing enthalpy influence phase stability.
Atomic size mismatch and mixing enthalpy influence the distribution of catalytically active sites.
The initial noble metal–based HEA nanomaterials have a random distribution of constituent elements.
Selecting different combinations of Pt, Pd, Au, Ag, Rh, and Ir can systematically vary atomic size mismatch and mixing enthalpy.
Atomic size mismatch and mixing enthalpy determine the thermodynamic and kinetic feasibility of forming a stable single-phase HEA structure.
Formation of a stable single-phase HEA structure affects the uniformity and availability of catalytically active sites.
Moderate atomic size mismatch and negative mixing enthalpy promote stable single-phase HEA structures.
Stable single-phase HEA structures produced under moderate size mismatch and negative mixing enthalpy have uniformly distributed active sites.
Uniformly distributed active sites lead to enhanced catalytic performance.
High atomic size mismatch or positive mixing enthalpy makes phase segregation more likely.
Phase-segregated materials produced under high size mismatch or positive mixing enthalpy exhibit reduced catalytic activity relative to materials with moderate mismatch and negative mixing enthalpy.
The proposed relationship applies only under synthesis conditions that permit sufficient atomic diffusion and mixing.
The proposed catalytic relationship applies to reactions for which active-site uniformity is critical.
The quantitative thresholds separating stable and unstable phases in terms of atomic size mismatch and mixing enthalpy are not well established.
The comparison should hold temperature, pressure, and precursor concentrations constant while varying elemental combinations.
Phase composition can be assessed by X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy, while catalytic performance can be assessed by turnover frequency and selectivity in CO oxidation.
Consistent formation of stable single phases with comparable or superior catalytic performance at high size mismatch or positive mixing enthalpy would falsify the hypothesis.
